extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, in-house patent counsel, and appellate practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes Federal Circuit standards and evidentiary criteria across patent-litigation issues (claim construction, doctrine of equivalents, willfulness, damages, §271(e)(1) safe harbor, expert testimony, PTAB practice). Useful for evaluating litigation strategy, trial proof, and appellate arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skinny-label / Hatch-Waxman balance for induced infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity and consistency in a generic manufacturer's communications regarding a drug marketed under a skinny label may be essential in avoiding liability for induced infringement; courts acknowledge a 'careful balance struck by the Hatch-Waxman Act regarding section viii carve-outs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brand and generic interests are balanced by § viii carve-outs; to avoid induced-infringement exposure, communications about off-label/skinny-label uses should be clear and consistent. The court may treat label language itself as teaching an infringing use (see GSK context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction — use of extrinsic dictionaries and intrinsic evidence; forfeiture
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may construe technical terms (e.g., 'VoIP') by reference to industry-agreed plain and ordinary meaning and extrinsic technical dictionaries, but intrinsic evidence controls; failure to raise a proposed redefinition in district court may forfeit the argument on appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts can rely on technical dictionaries and expert evidence to construe terms; a party that claims a patentee redefined a term must timely raise that argument below or risk forfeiture. Court may reject expert testimony inconsistent with documentary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents — requirement for particularized testimony and linking argument
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove infringement under the doctrine of equivalents, a patentee must present particularized expert testimony and linking argument tying specific elements of the accused product to claim limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalized testimony about overall similarity is insufficient. Experts must (1) identify particular elements in the accused product that correspond to claim limitations and (2) provide a meaningful explanation under the function-way-result (or other) test explaining why those elements are equivalent. Failure to do so supports JMOL of non-infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function-way-result proof must include meaningful explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: When using the function-way-result test, expert testimony must provide a meaningful explanation of why each accused element is equivalent under each part of the test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passing references or aggregated descriptions (e.g., 'several button presses') that do not identify which components are equivalent and why do not satisfy the patentee’s burden. Jury cannot find equivalence if not told what components are equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insubstantial-differences formulation requires particularized proof
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'insubstantial differences' theory of equivalence likewise requires particularized testimony and linking argument regarding the insubstantiality of the differences between claimed invention and the accused device/process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentees must present an independent insubstantial-differences theory at trial with element-by-element linking; relying on general similarity testimony is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: No blanket exception for 'easily understandable' technologies in DOE cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit will not create a categorical exception excusing the requirement for particularized testimony and linking argument merely because the technology is 'easily understandable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy reasons (preventing jury overreach and preserving the doctrine's limits) underpin the uniform requirement regardless of complexity; litigators should not assume lay obviousness obviates evidentiary requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: JMOL and sufficiency-of-evidence standard in DOE and other contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court may set aside a jury verdict and grant judgment as a matter of law where the evidentiary record is inadequate to support the verdict (e.g., on doctrine-of-equivalents theories lacking particularized proof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate review examines whether the record contains sufficient particularized testimony and linking argument; absent that, JMOL is proper even where a jury found infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement — knowledge plus additional evidence required; §298 limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of an asserted patent and evidence of infringement are necessary but not sufficient for willfulness; 35 U.S.C. §298 prohibits using an accused infringer’s failure to seek advice of counsel as proof of willfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts should exclude testimony that relies on alleged failure to obtain counsel as an indicium of willfulness. Plaintiffs must present other evidence (objective indicia, egregious conduct, post-notice behavior) beyond mere knowledge and infringement to prove willfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney-fees/exceptionality — 'red flags' and totality-of-the-circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may find a case exceptional and award attorney fees based on the totality of the circumstances and the presence of 'red flags' indicating the suit was fatally flawed (e.g., adverse district-court decisions, relevant Federal Circuit decisions, PTAB findings, office actions, warning letters, weak expert analyses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all purported red flags suffice—non-precedential decisions or PTAB findings may at best signal known concepts but do not automatically establish exceptionality. Courts should perform side-by-side analyses and explain how each red flag supports a finding of frivolity or objective baselessness; mere disagreement among experts is typical and not dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entire Market Value Rule and apportionment for reasonable royalty damages
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty must apportion infringing and non-infringing features to arrive at a royalty base comprised of the smallest salable patent-practicing unit; using an entire multi-component product as the royalty base requires proof that the patented feature(s) were the basis of customer demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentees relying on the entire-market-value rule must present customer-centric evidence (market studies, consumer surveys, testimony) showing the patented feature drove demand. Conclusory technical-expert assertions that patented features drove demand are insufficient. Apportionment is required unless a comparable license already embodies proper apportionment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe-harbor of 35 U.S.C. §271(e)(1) — 'reasonably related' and 'solely' interpreted
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 271(e)(1) exempts acts 'solely for uses reasonably related to the development and submission of information' to the FDA; courts apply a 'reasonable basis for believing' standard to determine whether the use will produce information relevant to an FDA submission. 'Solely' does not require exclusivity of purpose; the statute covers acts that are reasonably related even if data may be used for other purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis is act-specific: for each asserted infringing act (including importation), the safe harbor is available only if that act bears a reasonable relation to FDA-submission-related information development. Intent or alternative uses are generally irrelevant. Importing alone, without actual use, can fall within the safe harbor if reasonably related to FDA submission activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence showing reasonable relation to FDA submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Documentary and testimonial proof of concrete steps toward FDA approval (e.g., clinical trial synopsis preparation, pre-submission drafts, communications with FDA, hiring FDA consultants, later filing of a PMA) supports application of §271(e)(1).'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may weigh whether a reasonably minded juror could infer the importation/use was wholly unrelated to FDA-submission activities; undisputed preparatory steps toward approval strengthen safe-harbor arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert witness qualification — ordinary skill in the art (no timing requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert testifying from the vantage of a person of ordinary skill in the art must, at minimum, possess ordinary skill in the art; the expert need not have acquired that skill level prior to the time of the alleged invention to testify from that vantage point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenges that an expert lacked requisite skill at the time of invention (timing-based disqualification) are disfavored; courts allow experts to testify about the POSITA perspective even if their credentials accrued later, provided they possess ordinary skill in the art overall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility and reliability of damages expert opinions (reasonable royalty/hypothetical negotiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A damages expert's hypothetical-negotiation royalty opinion must be sufficiently tied to the facts of the case (e.g., comparable licenses, licensing clauses, testimony) and employ a reliable methodology including appropriate apportionment or a demonstrably comparable license that embodies apportionment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparable licenses used as anchors must be economically and technically comparable; where comparability exists, built-in apportionment may obviate separate apportionment analysis. Disputes about comparability and reliability are factual issues for cross-examination and the jury, not always grounds for exclusion. The absence of documentary calculations tying lump-sum settlements to per-unit rates may support challenge but is not dispositive if other evidence ties the rate to the facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: WesternGeco extraterritoriality framework applies to reasonable-royalty damages under §271(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: The WesternGeco two-step framework (rebut presumption against extraterritoriality; if not rebutted, determine whether the case involves a domestic application of the statute) governs extraterritoriality analysis for damages arising under §271(a), not only §271(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patentee seeks to base a royalty award on foreign conduct, it must show how that foreign conduct increases the value of the domestic infringement while respecting apportionment limits. Damages theories focusing on non-infringing foreign conduct risk exclusion under this framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB joinder and limitations on joined-party participation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may permit joinder of a time-barred party but impose procedural restrictions (e.g., consolidated filings, reliance on current petitioner for testimony, limitations on deposition/hearing time) to minimize delay and complication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joined parties may be restricted in their ability to introduce new procedural burdens; parties seeking to join should expect the Board to condition participation to protect efficient resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions to amend in IPR — scope of permissible opposing arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory limit that only grounds in the petition be considered does not apply in the same way to motions to amend; when a patent owner introduces new claims, the Board may consider arguments, including those based on references not in the original petition, to oppose the proposed substitute claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A time-barred or previously non-participating party (e.g., a joinder) may be permitted to oppose a revised motion to amend and rely on additional prior art to show the proposed claims would be unpatentable. Patent owners seeking to amend should be prepared to face broader opposition arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation-to-combine and substantial-evidence standard at PTAB
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may find proposed substitute claims unpatentable as obvious based on a motivation-to-combine supported by expert testimony (e.g., that a skilled artisan would look to a reference's method/algorithm to address a need), and the Federal Circuit reviews such findings for substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board reliance on experts to establish what a skilled artisan would do is permissible; appellants must show lack of substantial evidence to overturn the PTAB. When challenging PTAB obviousness findings, courts expect a record-level engagement with the references and expert testimony.
